title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Open-source application portfolio management Know every application, and what to do with it AppWren is one living record of every application an organization runs: who answers for it, what it is for, what it is built on, what it costs, and how healthy it is. From that record it works out a recommendation for each one, and shows the reasoning. Get started Try the demo Source on GitHub

title: Overview
heading: The reasoning is on the screen
text: Every score opens to its factors, levels, weights, and sources, and every recommendation to the rule that produced it. Nothing is typed in as a verdict.

title: Overview
heading: People decide
text: The system recommends. A named person records what will be done and why. Where the two differ, both are shown, and neither overwrites the other.

title: Overview
heading: Unknown is not zero
text: A fact nobody has recorded is left out of the score and counted against confidence. Too little known means Assess , never a guess.

title: Overview
heading: Quiet by design
text: No scanners, collectors, or agents, and no access to anything else on the network. It records what people know and decide. Scores

title: Overview
heading: Four scores, each with its working
text: Business value, technical health, cost and burden, and risk exposure are worked out from the record and from what assessors answered. Each opens to the factors behind it, the level each stands at, its weight, and where the fact came from. Beside them is data confidence: how much of each score's weight is known, and which missing facts would raise it most, each with a link to where it is entered. How a score is worked out Recommendations

title: Overview
heading: A recommendation, and the rule behind it
text: Invest, maintain, tolerate, modernize, replace, consolidate, retire, incubate, or assess: rules are tried in order, and the record names the one that matched. A guardrail protects what must not go without a successor. A Retire for the only provider of a capability, or for a system of record for regulated information, becomes Replace , and the working says why. Recommendations Decisions

title: Overview
heading: A decision is a person's, with a reason and a date
text: Whoever leads the unit, or the portfolio team, records the disposition: what will be done, why, by when, and when to look again. The scores as they stood that day are kept with it. A decision that differs from the recommendation is not an error. It is listed as a mismatch with its reason, so a review starts from the cases worth talking about. Decisions and mismatches Overlap

title: Overview
heading: What are we paying for twice?
text: Applications are mapped to the capabilities they serve. Every capability served by more than one is listed with those applications side by side: scores, recommendation, decision, how many people use each, and what each costs. Name a primary provider, and the others that are worth less are recommended for consolidation. Overlap Impact

title: Overview
heading: What breaks if this goes?
text: Before a retirement is recommended, an application's Connections say what it would touch: what depends on it, directly and in turn, the interfaces that would stop, and the capabilities left with nothing behind them. It also says which units use it, up to how many people, and what its record says must outlive it, such as active studies or data that must be kept. What breaks if this goes Data flows

title: Overview
heading: Follow a class of data from system to system
text: An interface records data passing from one application to another: by what method, how often, and which classes of data it carries. Choose a class to see every interface that carries it and every application that holds it. Where an interface delivers a class the receiving application's record does not list, the flow is marked, because that application's risk is understated until someone settles it. Follow a class of data Lifecycle

title: Overview
heading: What falls out of support, and what runs on it
text: Components are built on technology releases, and each release has a day its support ends. The timeline shows the releases in use, soonest first, with how many components in how many applications are on each. Support dates can be typed, or brought in from a file of end-of-life data that you supply. An application on a release past its date scores worse for it, and one that also holds restricted data is flagged. Lifecycle Cost

title: Overview
heading: What it costs, line by line, and who pays
text: An application's cost is a list of lines: a license, hosting, a support contract, your own people's time, each with what pays for it. A grant has an end date, and an application paid for by one that ends within a year is flagged until someone decides what becomes of it. Contracts carry their renewal and notice dates and whether a data agreement is in place. Cost and contracts are shown only to those who may see them, and a total is given whole or not at all. Cost and contracts Capabilities

title: Overview
heading: The capability map, measured
text: The map shows what the organization does, and how many applications stand behind each part of it: none, one, or an overlap. Measure it by any score, by data confidence, or by the health of the weakest application behind each capability, since a capability is as exposed as the worst thing it rests on. The capability map, measured Connections

title: Overview
heading: What is this connected to?
text: Every record opens to a picture of what it is joined to: what it depends on, where its data goes, the capabilities it serves, what it is built on, where it runs, and the contracts and funding behind it. A list beside the picture says the same in full, and all of it works from the keyboard. Records the reader may not see are counted, never named. How a record is connected Data handling

title: Overview
heading: Which applications hold health data, and how well are they kept?
text: Choose a class of data and get the applications that handle it, with what an analysis of risk asks about each: who answers for it, where it runs, how people sign in, the support state of what it is built on, and whether a data agreement is in place. The same rows export as a spreadsheet. Who handles a class of data Home

title: Overview
heading: One page of what each person owes
text: Most people who keep an application are not portfolio specialists. Home lists what is theirs to do: an application never assessed or whose assessment has expired, a flag on one of theirs, a record that lacks what its stage requires. The dashboard gives the portfolio team the whole: recommendations beside decisions, flags, confidence, and what everything costs, with every figure a link to the list it counts. Home and the dashboard

title: Overview
heading: One definition of an application
text: Applications, their components, and where each runs are separate records, so the portfolio compares like with like.

title: Overview
heading: Judged by the right rubric
text: A shared platform is judged on what rests on it, and research software on whether it can be kept going. A pilot is not judged on use at all.

title: Overview
heading: Ready for research
text: Grant funding and its end dates, studies that depend on an application, research data classes, and software kept by one person are all part of the record.

title: Overview
heading: Working on the first day
text: The vocabularies, a starter capability map of 43 capabilities, a question bank, and a scoring model with its profiles, rules, and flags come with a new installation.

title: Overview
heading: A program you can change
text: The questions, weights, thresholds, and rules are yours to change. Each version is kept, and every assessment and snapshot names the one it used.

title: Overview
heading: A history that holds
text: Every change is in an append-only, hash-chained log, with who made it. An auditor reads everything and changes nothing.

title: Overview
heading: The portfolio as it stood
text: A snapshot keeps every application's scores, recommendation, and decision on a day, so a review can be compared with the one before.

title: Overview
heading: In and out
text: Applications come in from a spreadsheet, with a dry run that reports every problem by row. Every list exports as CSV, and as JSON through the API.

title: Overview
heading: Who sees what
text: Roles are held over units. Sensitive fields, costs, and contracts are withheld from those who may not see them, in every list, figure, and export.

title: Overview
heading: Where it runs
text: Hosting platforms list everything on them by environment: what would stop if a data center or a cloud account were lost.

title: Overview
heading: Sign in your way
text: Local accounts out of the box. Optional single sign-on by OpenID Connect, built to work with Microsoft Entra ID, with roles and units taken from the provider.

title: Overview
heading: Open and yours
text: Apache 2.0 with no paid edition. SQLite on a laptop or PostgreSQL on a server, no build step, and your own name and colors.

title: Overview
heading: Try it
text: You need uv , which provides the right Python. Clone the repository and build the demo organization: a fictional research institute with a clinic, two years of history, 107 applications, three survey tools doing one job, a grant about to end, a database release reaching the end of its support, and a decision that differs from its recommendation. git clone https://github.com/robert-mcdermott/appwren.git cd appwren uv sync uv run appwren demo uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve Open http://127.0.0.1:8020 . The sign-in page offers eight sample people and asks for no password. Start as the portfolio manager. Explore the demo organization says who to try next, and Getting started sets

title: Getting started
heading: Getting started
text: Getting started This guide takes you from nothing to a running AppWren that your organization can sign in to. It is for whoever installs it and sets it up. Allow about fifteen minutes. If you only want to look around first, skip to Explore the demo organization .

title: Getting started
heading: What you need
text: uv , which provides the right Python (3.12 or later). A copy of this repository. Every command in these guides is run through uv run appwren … from the repository directory. The full list is in the command reference .

title: Getting started
heading: Install
text: uv sync

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the installation
text: uv run appwren init init does five things: Writes appwren.toml , the deployment settings, in the current directory. Creates the data home, ./var , which holds everything that is not in the database. Creates the database. With no other setting, this is a SQLite file inside the data home. Loads the default program: the vocabularies (lifecycle stages, sourcing, tiers, data classes, interface methods, environments, cost categories, and the rest), what each lifecycle stage requires of a record, which fields are sensitive, a starter capability map of 43 capabilities, a question bank of nine questions, and the scoring model with its three profiles, rules, guardrails, and flags. Asks for your email

title: Getting started
heading: Check it
text: uv run appwren doctor doctor checks the configuration, the data home, that the database answers, that its schema is the one this version expects, that the database still refuses changes to the history, and that the history verifies. It exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Getting started
heading: Run it
text: uv run appwren serve The server prints its address, by default http://127.0.0.1:8000 . Use --port to pick another port. serve refuses to start in three cases, and says what to do in each: It says Do this The database schema is behind uv run appwren db upgrade There is no administrator yet uv run appwren users add you@example.org --name "Your Name" --role admin The port is already in use Stop what is using it, or pass --port As installed, AppWren listens only on the machine it runs on. To put it in front of other people, read Configuration first.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in for the first time
text: Open the address in a browser and sign in with the email address and password you gave init . AppWren signs in with local accounts: an email address and a password that it keeps. Nothing else has to be installed or connected. Signing in with your organization's identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID, is optional and can be added at any time: see Single sign-on . Five failed attempts within fifteen minutes stop sign-in for that account from that address for a few minutes. A sign-in ends after 12 hours without activity, and after 7 days in any case. Both are settings . To change your password, open the account menu at the top right and choose Your account . Changing it signs out your ot

title: Getting started
heading: Set up the organization
text: The administrator account sets the installation up. It does not keep applications or record decisions: that belongs to the roles below, and an administrator who also does that work is given a second role.

title: Getting started
heading: Units
text: Admin → Units holds the organization as a hierarchy of any depth: divisions, departments, centers, core facilities, labs, clinics, offices, and teams. Every application belongs to a unit, roles can be limited to a unit and everything beneath it, and figures roll up the tree. Give each unit a short code; imports refer to units by it.

title: Getting started
heading: People and roles
text: Admin → People adds accounts and gives them roles. A person with no role is a member: they can read the catalog, and they keep the applications they are named on. Role What it is for Manager The portfolio team. Edits any application, records decisions, takes snapshots, and shapes the program. Can be limited to a unit Architect Keeps the records the whole organization shares (capabilities, technologies, vendors, hosting platforms, and funding sources) and assesses applications. Can be limited to a unit Leader Leads a unit. Sees it and everything beneath it, and records decisions for its applications Steward Keeps a unit's applications complete and current: adds, edits, imports, and assesses t

title: Getting started
heading: Import units and people
text: Both screens take a CSV file, which is the quick way to load an organization. Each import can be run dry first and reports every problem by row, so nothing is half-loaded. The import dialog shows the columns it expects.

title: Getting started
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance sets the product's name, your organization's name, a logo, an accent color, and the default palette. See Running the program .

title: Getting started
heading: Bring in your applications
text: Most organizations start from a spreadsheet. Applications → Import reads a CSV file, matches its columns to AppWren's fields, and runs dry first, reporting every problem by row. A row with a reference already on record updates that application; any other row adds one. See Import and export . Then give the stewards of each unit a week to fill the gaps. Reports → Data quality shows, unit by unit, what is missing.

title: Getting started
heading: Explore the demo organization
text: To see AppWren with data in it before you set anything up, build the demo: uv run appwren demo # builds ./demo uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve # runs it at http://127.0.0.1:8020 The demo is the Bramblewood Institute for Health Research, a fictional research institute with a clinic and two years of history: 57 units, about 180 people, 107 applications (about forty of them research tools kept by labs), about 120 components, 24 technologies, 24 interfaces, 87 deployments on six hosting platforms, 22 contracts, about 125 assessments, 65 decisions, and four quarterly portfolio snapshots. There is an application to modernize with three flags, three survey tools doing one job, a gra

title: The portfolio
heading: The portfolio
text: The portfolio This guide is for everyone who keeps, assesses, or reads the record of an application: the people named on applications, the stewards of units, architects, leaders, and the portfolio team. It covers what an application is, the record and what each stage of its life requires, components and what they are built on, capabilities, assessment, the scores and the working behind them, recommendations, flags, decisions, cost and contracts, and import and export. What joins applications to one another is in The landscape .

title: The portfolio
heading: What counts as an application
text: An application is software, or a service built from software, that people name, use for a purpose, and could decide to keep, change, or retire as one thing. An application Not an application The grants management system A server or a database on its own: record it as a component of what it serves The learning management system A report or a module of a larger system: a component of that system A lab's sample tracker, used by three labs A spreadsheet one person keeps for themselves The research data warehouse A programming language or a platform: a technology Holding to one definition is what lets the portfolio compare like with like. The definition is part of the program, and the form for a

title: The portfolio
heading: The record
text: Portfolio → Applications lists every application you may see, with its scores, its recommendation, and the decision on record. Filter it by lifecycle stage, sourcing, tier, domain, or unit; search by name or reference; and choose Mine for those you are named on. Each application has a permanent reference, such as APP-0042 , that never changes or is reused. Its page has nine parts: Part What it holds Overview The scores, the recommendation and the decision, the people named on it, what its record still needs, and every field Scores Each dimension's working, the rule behind the recommendation, and what would raise confidence Assessment The latest answers, who gave them and when, and every asse

title: The portfolio
heading: The fields
text: Besides its name, its summary, and its unit, an application's fields come in sections: Section Fields What it is Lifecycle stage and since when; sourcing (SaaS, Commercial run here, Built here, Open source run here, Low-code, Research software, or Vendor-hosted custom); purpose (Mission, Operations, Insight, Foundation); pace (Steady, Evolving, Experimental); domain; criticality tier, from 1 (mission critical) to 5 (minimal); other names it goes by Where it comes from Vendor, product, edition or version, hosting, its address, and its documentation Who uses it About how many people use it, and whether people outside the organization do Who supports it How many people can maintain it, and the

title: The portfolio
heading: People named on it
text: Every application has exactly one accountable owner , the person who answers for it. Whoever adds an application is accountable for it until they hand it on. Others may be named as business owner, technical owner, product manager, support contact, data steward, security contact, or executive sponsor, and as many of each as it needs. Anyone named on an application may change who else is named. Only the accountable owner, the steward of its unit, or an architect or manager whose scope includes it may hand on the accountability. An application whose accountable owner has left is flagged No accountable owner and listed on its steward's home page.

title: The portfolio
heading: What each stage requires
text: An application moves through eight lifecycle stages: Proposed, Evaluating, Phase-in, Active, Containment, Phase-out, Retired, and Archived. Each stage asks more of the record than the one before, and the record says what is still missing, now and before the next stage: Stage Requires, in addition to the stages before Proposed A summary, its sourcing, and the capabilities it serves Evaluating An accountable owner, its purpose, and its data classes Phase-in Its tier, hosting, supporting unit, annual cost, and funding Active How people sign in, monitoring, backup, users, maintainers, domain, pace, what its components are built on, and a current assessment Containment A decision about what to do

title: The portfolio
heading: Links and other systems
text: An application can be recorded as depending on another, as part of another, or as replacing another. Data passing between two applications is recorded as an interface . How many active applications depend on one, by a link or by receiving its data, is part of its business value. It can also carry its references in other systems: a configuration item, a ticket queue, a repository, its sign-in registration, a contract number, or a governance record. Search finds an application by any of them, and each is shown as a link where the program gives its system an address pattern .

title: The portfolio
heading: Restricted applications
text: An application can be marked restricted , which hides even its existence from everyone except the people named on it, the stewards and leaders of its unit, architects and managers whose scope includes it, auditors, and administrators. Use it sparingly: a portfolio is useful in proportion to how many people can find what already exists.

title: The portfolio
heading: Components and what they are built on
text: Portfolio → Components lists the parts of applications: services, web front ends, databases, batch jobs, integrations, reports, modules, libraries, mobile apps, analysis pipelines, and infrastructure. A component belongs to one application and takes its unit and its visibility from it. Each component records the technologies it is built on, and which release of each. That is what makes technology currency a fact rather than an opinion: AppWren knows when each release reaches end of support. Landscape → Technologies holds the languages, frameworks, runtimes, databases, operating systems, platforms, and products the organization uses, each with its releases and their support dates, its vendor,

title: The portfolio
heading: Capabilities
text: A capability is something the organization does, such as Biospecimen tracking or Participant surveys , named for what it does, not for the software that does it. Landscape → Capabilities shows the capability map: the default program's 43 capabilities in five areas (Research, Clinical care, Education, Administration, and Information technology), each with how many applications serve it. An application's Capabilities part says which it serves. Where several serve one, one of them can be named its primary provider. This is how AppWren finds overlap: an application that serves a capability whose primary is another, is primary for none, and is worth less than that primary, is recommended for Cons

title: The portfolio
heading: Assessment
text: An assessment is a set of answers to the question bank, given by a named person on a date. The questions are kept for judgment; anything that can be measured is a field instead. Dimension Questions Business value How closely does it support what the organization is trying to achieve? How well does it do what its users need today? Will the organization still need what it does in three years? Technical health How well does it meet the service its users expect? How easy is it to change, upgrade, and keep current? How confident are we in the vendor and the product's future? (asked only of vendor-sourced applications) Cost and burden How much effort does it take to keep running? How much effort d

title: The portfolio
heading: The scores
text: Every application in service has four scores, each from 1 to 5, where 5 is always best for the organization : Score Asks 5 means Business value How much would the organization lose without it? A great deal Technical health How well is it built, run, and kept current? Very well Cost and burden What does it take to keep? Little Risk exposure What could go wrong while it is kept? Little Each score is the weighted average of its factors . A factor comes from an answer ( strategic fit ), from a field ( criticality from the tier, security from the sign-in method), from a number in bands ( reach : fewer than 10 users is 1, at least 1,000 is 5), or from a calculation over the record ( technology cur

title: The portfolio
heading: Unknown is not zero
text: A factor with no data is left out of its score, never assumed. The score is worked out from what is known, and coverage says how much of the score's weight that was. A score with less than half its weight known is thin : it is shown, with its coverage, and it cannot carry a recommendation. Data confidence is the average coverage of the four scores. Below 70%, the recommendation is Assess . Beside it, AppWren lists what would raise confidence : each unknown factor, the heaviest first, with a link to where it is entered. A factor can also be not applicable : vendor viability for software built here, or technology currency for a SaaS product. It is left out of the score and of the weight confid

title: The portfolio
heading: The working
text: Choose any score to see how it was worked out: each factor, its level, its weight, and why it has that level ( Answered in the assessment ; 380 people: bands 10, 50, 250, 1,000 ; The only active application for Biospecimen management ), with any factor that is unknown or not applicable and the reason, and the sum. The Scores part shows the same for all four at once, with the assessment the answers came from and who gave it. Every figure can be redone by hand from what the screen shows.

title: The portfolio
heading: Profiles
text: Not every application is judged by the same rubric. The scoring model has three profiles , and the first that matches applies: Profile Applies to What differs Foundation Shared platforms (purpose Foundation) Judged on what rests on them: reach and dependents weigh more Research software Sourcing Research software Judged on whether it can be kept going: sustainability and maintainability weigh more Standard Everything else Some facts also set a floor : an application that active studies depend on, or that is a system of record for regulated information, has business value of at least 4.0. The working names the floor and why.

title: The portfolio
heading: Recommendations
text: The scores, the lifecycle stage, and the record together give a recommended disposition . Rules are tried in order, and the first that matches gives the recommendation; the Scores part names it. Disposition When it is recommended What it means Incubate Proposed, Evaluating, or Phase-in; or experimental and under a year old New; not yet judged on use Assess Confidence under 70%, or value or health thin Not enough is known to say Consolidate It does what a capability's primary provider does, and is worth less Move its users to the primary Invest Value and health at least 3.0, and cost and burden at least 3.0 Grow its capability and use Maintain Value and health at least 3.0, but costly to keep

title: The portfolio
heading: The portfolio chart
text: Portfolio → Portfolio chart places every scored application by business value against technical health, or against cost and burden. Each bubble is sized by its cost, where you may see costs, and colored by risk exposure. The threshold lines divide it into the quarters the rules use. A table beneath gives the exact figures for every application on the chart, and the applications too little is known about to place are listed after it.

title: The portfolio
heading: Flags
text: Flags are raised whatever the recommendation. Each is a separate signal, with its own words, and names the facts that raised it. Flag When Restricted data on unsupported technology It holds restricted data, and something it runs on is past end of support No accountable owner Nobody answers for it Grant ending It is paid for by a grant that ends within a year, and nobody has decided what to do with it this year One person keeps this Built here, low-code, or research software, tier 1 to 3, with one maintainer or none Assessment expired Its latest assessment is no longer current Decision review due The decision on record is past its review date Archive before retiring It is to be retired, repla

title: The portfolio
heading: Decisions
text: The engine recommends; a person decides. A decision records a disposition for an application by a named person, with a rationale, a date to review it (a year on, unless you choose another), and, if you wish, a target date. A decision to consolidate names the application its users will move to. Managers record decisions for any application, and leaders for the applications of their units. Nobody records a decision about an application they are accountable for. To record one, open the application and choose Record a decision . The dialog shows the recommendation and its working beside the choice. A decision may be any disposition, whatever the recommendation: people know things the scores cann

title: The portfolio
heading: Mismatches
text: When today's recommendation differs from the decision on record, the application shows a mismatch : both dispositions side by side, each with its working. A mismatch changes nothing on its own; it is a prompt for the next portfolio review. Portfolio → Decisions lists them, beside the decisions whose review date has come and the applications nobody has decided about yet.

title: The portfolio
heading: What it costs
text: An application's Cost part says what it costs a year, and how much that is for each person who uses it. The figure can be typed on the record as a rough estimate, or broken down into cost lines : A line says What it is for A license or subscription, hosting, a support contract, your own people's time, or something else How much a year What pays for it A funding source : an operating budget, a grant, a chargeback, a capital project The contract it falls under Optional. Naming one makes that contract cover the application Choose Break it down , or Edit the lines , to change them. Once an application has lines, its annual cost is their sum , and the figure on the record can no longer be typed o

title: The portfolio
heading: Funding sources
text: Funding sources are kept by architects and managers, under Portfolio → Contracts → Funding sources . Each has a kind, a code such as a cost center or grant number, and, for a grant or a project, the day the money stops. Its page lists what it pays for.

title: The portfolio
heading: Contracts
text: Portfolio → Contracts holds the agreements with vendors that applications run under: Vendor, number, start, and end The end is the end of the current term Notice, in days How long before the end the vendor must be told, if it is not to renew. The list shows the date this makes, and marks it when it is within 90 days or has passed Renews by itself Whether it renews unless someone says otherwise Yearly value and licenses bought Data agreement Whether an agreement covers the data the vendor handles: in place, not needed, or missing What it covers The applications, and how many of the licenses each uses Narrow the list to contracts ending within 90 days, six months, or a year. Stewards, architec

title: The portfolio
heading: Import applications
text: Applications → Import reads a CSV file: Choose the file. AppWren reads its header and guesses which column is which field; correct any guess, or leave a column out. Run it dry. Every problem is reported by row and column, and nothing is saved. Import. All the rows are saved, or none of them. A row whose reference is already on record updates that application, through the same checks as an edit by hand. Any other row adds one. The accountable owner is given by email address, and the vendor by name. A row that names nobody accountable is imported, and its application is flagged No accountable owner . A value for a sensitive field you may not see is refused. Stewards, architects, and managers i

title: The portfolio
heading: Export
text: Every list can be exported as CSV from its Export button: applications, components, interfaces, deployments, contracts, funding sources, vendors, technologies, hosting platforms, capabilities, the applications that handle a class of data, and, from a list that a dashboard figure opens, the portfolio with its scores, recommendations, and decisions. The same exports come as JSON through the API . An export holds only what you may see, with the filters you have chosen. Values that a spreadsheet would treat as a formula are prefixed so that they are shown as text, and each export is recorded in the history.

title: The portfolio
heading: Next
text: To see the whole portfolio's figures and what is missing from its records, read Running the program . To connect another system, read the API guide .

title: The landscape
heading: The landscape
text: The landscape This guide is for architects, the portfolio team, and anyone who needs to see an application in its surroundings: what it exchanges with others and what data passes, what depends on it, where it runs, what else does the same job, and what it is built on that is falling out of support. The portfolio covers one application's record; this guide covers what joins them.

title: The landscape
heading: Interfaces
text: An interface is data passing from one application to another. It is a record of its own, with a reference such as INT-0015 , and says: From and To The application the data comes from, and the one it goes to. Two different applications Method An API call, a file transfer, a scheduled extract and load, a shared database, messages or events, an embedded page, or by hand How often As it happens, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or when someone asks Data it carries The classes of data that pass, from the same list an application's record uses Owner Who to ask about it To record one, open either application, choose Connections , and then It sends data or It receives data . title: The landscape
heading: A consumer depends on its source
text: An application that receives data depends on the one that sends it, just as a recorded depends on link says. Both count, once each, toward the source's dependents , which is part of its business value. Recording what a system feeds can therefore raise its score, and its working says how many depend on it.

title: The landscape
heading: Follow a class of data
text: Landscape → Data flows shows where each class of data travels. Choose a class to see every interface that carries it and every application that holds it. Where an interface delivers a class that the receiving application's record does not list, the flow is marked. Either the interface carries less than was recorded, or the application's record needs the class added. AppWren cannot know which, and changes neither; but until somebody does, that application's risk exposure is understated, because it is worked out from the classes its record lists.

title: The landscape
heading: How a record is connected

Open it with How it is connected on the record, or The picture on an application's Connections. The record is in the middle, with its neighbors in groups: what it depends on and what depends on it, where its data goes and comes from, the capabilities it serves, its components, what they are built on, its vendor, where it runs, and the contracts and funding behind it. title: The landscape

Read it before recommending a retirement. A Retire for the only provider of a capability is already turned into Replace by the engine; this p

title: The landscape
heading: Where it runs
text: Landscape → Hosting holds the hosting platforms things run on: data centers, cloud accounts, compute clusters, hosting providers, a vendor's own service, or people's own computers. Architects and managers keep them, each with its kind, its provider, and where it is. A deployment says that an application, or one of its components, runs in an environment (production, staging, test, development, or disaster recovery) on a platform, optionally at an address. To record one, open the application, choose Components , then Say where it runs . Leave the name empty and it is named for what runs and where: Tracker API, production . A platform's page lists everything on it, by environment: what would st

title: The landscape
heading: Overlap
text: Landscape → Overlap lists every capability served by more than one application in service, with those applications side by side: their four scores, the recommendation, the decision on record, how many people use each, and what each costs where you may see it. The primary provider is named first. An application that serves a capability whose primary is another, and is worth less, is recommended for Consolidate . Where no primary is named, none of them is recommended for consolidation: name one on its Capabilities part. As a list opens the same applications in the portfolio list, where they can be exported. A total of cost is shown only when you may see the cost of every application in it.

title: The landscape
heading: The capability map, measured
text: Landscape → Capabilities shows the map. Above it, choose what to measure each capability by: Measure Shows How many serve it The number of applications in service: none, one, or an overlap Business value, Technical health, Cost and burden, Risk exposure The average over the applications that serve it Weakest health The technical health of the weakest application that serves it: a capability is as exposed as the worst thing it rests on Data confidence How much is known about the applications that serve it Each figure is a number with the score's own bar, and opens the applications it was worked out from. A broader capability is measured over every application beneath it, each counted once.

title: The landscape
heading: Lifecycle
text: Landscape → Lifecycle shows the technology releases applications run on, soonest end of support first. Each is a bar from the release's first day to the end of its support, with today marked, and beside it the state, the date, and how many components in how many applications are on it. Narrow it to what is past its end of support, ending within a year, or supported. Every release on record adds the releases nothing runs on. Applications with a planned retirement are listed beneath. The counts here are the same as on each technology's page, which names the applications.

title: The landscape
heading: Radar
text: Radar , reached from Technologies or Lifecycle, shows the technologies in use by the organization's view of each for new work: Adopt , Trial , Assess , or Hold , each with its kind and how many components run on it. Technologies that are in use and that nobody has placed are listed apart: someone should say whether new work may use them. An application all of whose technologies are supported scores better for technology currency if every one is Adopt , and worse if any is on Hold .

title: The landscape
heading: Support dates from a file
text: Support dates can be typed on each technology's page, or brought in from a file so that nobody types them. AppWren does not fetch the file: you bring it. On each technology, set its End-of-life key : the name the file knows it by, such as python or postgresql . Get a JSON file of end-of-life data. It is one object: each product's key, with its list of releases. `` json { "python": [ {"cycle": "3.13", "releaseDate": "2024-10-07", "eol": "2029-10-31", "latest": "3.13.1"}, {"cycle": "3.9", "releaseDate": "2020-10-05", "eol": "2025-10-31"} ] } `` eol is the day support ends; extendedSupport , where it is a date, is the day extended support ends. On Landscape → Technologies , choose Import suppor

title: The landscape
heading: Who handles a class of data
text: Reports → Data handling lists the applications in service that handle a chosen class of data, with what an analysis of risk asks about each: Column What it says Application Its tier, unit, and sourcing Accountable Who answers for it, or that nobody does Where it runs Its platforms in production, or its hosting, and its vendor Sign-in How people sign in to it Built on The worst support state among what its components run on, and the releases Carries it How many interfaces carry the class into it and out of it Data agreement Whether a contract that covers it has one in place, needs none, or lacks one Export gives the same rows as a spreadsheet. title: Running the program
heading: Running the program
text: Running the program This guide is for the portfolio team and for administrators. It covers who may do what, who sees what, the program and how to change it, upgrading, the dashboard and data quality, portfolio snapshots, the history, appearance, and backing up.

title: Running the program
heading: Two kinds of authority
text: AppWren keeps judgment and administration apart. Managers run the portfolio. They keep any application, record decisions, take snapshots, and shape the program: the vocabularies, the fields, the questions, and the scoring model. Administrators run the installation: accounts, units, sign-in, and appearance. Administration does not by itself let anyone keep applications or record decisions. An administrator who also does that work holds a second role, and the history shows which they acted under.

title: Running the program
heading: Roles and scope
text: Everyone who can sign in is a member . The other six roles are given under Admin → People , or from the identity provider (see Single sign-on ). Role Scope May Member Their own applications Read the catalog, scores, recommendations, and decisions; keep and assess the applications they are named on Steward A unit and everything beneath it Add, edit, import, and assess its applications, and hand on who is accountable; record their interfaces, deployments, and cost lines; add contracts Leader A unit and everything beneath it See it, read its sensitive fields, cost lines, and contracts, and record decisions for its applications Architect The whole organization, or a unit Keep capabilities, techn

title: Running the program
heading: Who sees what
text: The catalog is open. Every application, component, interface, deployment, capability, technology, hosting platform, funding source, and vendor is visible to everyone signed in, with each application's scores, recommendation, and decision. A portfolio is useful in proportion to how many people can find what already exists: a researcher looking for an approved tool, an engineer checking who else runs a database, a team about to buy what another department already has. Two things narrow that. Sensitive fields. By default annual cost, the sign-in method, backup, and the last restore test are sensitive. They are visible to the people named on the application, to stewards, leaders, and architects

title: Running the program
heading: Shape the program
text: The program is everything the portfolio team configures, kept in the database rather than in a file on the server: Part What it holds Vocabularies Lifecycle stages, sourcing, purpose, pace, domains, tiers, hosting, sign-in methods, monitoring, backup, funding, data classes and their sensitivity, kinds of component, vendor, technology, platform, and unit, the radar's rings, the roles people hold on an application, link kinds, interface methods and frequencies, environments, cost categories, the states of a data agreement, other systems, and the dispositions Fields The organization's own fields, each in a section of the application's form What each stage requires The fields and records an appl

title: Running the program
heading: Change the program with a pack
text: In this release the program is changed as a file, by whoever runs the server: export it, edit it, check it, and load it. uv run appwren program export -o program.json # edit program.json uv run appwren program import program.json --dry-run uv run appwren program import program.json The whole pack is checked before anything is loaded, and nothing is loaded unless all of it can be: every vocabulary a field names, every fact a rule reads, every weight in a profile. --dry-run says what would change and changes nothing. A vocabulary value that is in use is retired rather than removed: records keep it, and it is no longer offered. Capabilities are only ever added. Rename or retire one in the app.

title: Running the program
heading: Links to other systems
text: An application can carry its identifier in another system: a configuration item, a ticket queue, a repository. To have each shown as a link, give the system an address pattern in the external_systems vocabulary of the pack, with {id} where the identifier goes: {"key": "repository", "label": "Repository", "url": "https://code.example.org/{id}"} A pattern must begin https:// . A pack with any other pattern is refused.

title: Running the program
heading: Versions
text: The question bank and the scoring model are versioned . A version in use is never changed: loading a pack that changes either publishes a new version, and the old one stays, marked superseded. Every assessment names the version of the questions it answered, and every snapshot names the version of the model it used, so a decision made last year still shows exactly what its maker saw. Changing the scoring model changes every application's scores at once, the next time they are read. Take a portfolio snapshot first if you want a record of the portfolio as it was. Editing the program in the app arrives in a later release; see the roadmap .

title: Running the program
heading: What an upgrade does to the program
text: uv run appwren db upgrade adds whatever is new in the default program and never overwrites what you have shaped. New vocabularies arrive with their defaults. A vocabulary you have changed is left as you have it. The scoring model. Version 0.2.0 has a new default model: cost and burden is now annual cost 30, cost per user 15, license use 10, support effort 25, and change effort 20, and there are two new flags. If you are still running the previous default unchanged, the upgrade publishes the new one as a new version, and scores for cost and burden move. If you have shaped your model, it is kept as it is. To take the new factors, export the default from a fresh installation or copy them from t

title: Running the program
heading: Read the dashboard
text: Reports → Dashboard shows the whole portfolio, or one unit and everything beneath it, or one domain. The headline: applications in service, how many have a decision, mismatches between decision and recommendation, reviews that are due, low confidence, and what runs on technology past or near its end of support. Recommendations and decisions: how many of each disposition, side by side, and how many have no decision yet. Lifecycle and sourcing: where the portfolio is in its life, and where its software comes from. Flags: how many applications carry each. Confidence: how many applications are known well enough to judge, in four bands. What it costs a year, and what pays for it: by kind of cost

title: Running the program
heading: Home
text: Home is each person's page of what is waiting on them: applications they are named on that have not been assessed or whose assessment has expired, flags on them, and what their records lack. A steward or manager also sees the applications in scope that nobody is accountable for; a leader or manager, the applications in their units waiting on a decision.

title: Running the program
heading: Data quality
text: Reports → Data quality shows, unit by unit, how complete the records are: applications with nobody accountable, no capability, no assessment, an expired assessment, low confidence, or something missing that their stage requires. Each figure opens its list. Choose a unit to see only it and the units beneath it. A portfolio's recommendations are only as good as its records, and this page is how the work of keeping them is shared out: give each steward the row for their unit.

title: Running the program
heading: Portfolio snapshots
text: A portfolio snapshot keeps every application's scores, recommendation, and working as they were on a day, under a name such as 2026 Q4 . Managers take them from Portfolio → Decisions → Snapshots with Take a snapshot , typically before each portfolio review and before changing the scoring model. A snapshot reopens unchanged after the applications or the program have changed. Its digest is recorded in the history, so a snapshot altered afterwards is detectable. Every decision also keeps a snapshot of the one application it was made about.

title: Running the program
heading: The history
text: Every change to every record is written to an append-only history in the same transaction as the change: who, when, and each value before and after. Each event is hashed together with the one before it, and the database itself refuses updates and deletes on the history. Each record's History part shows its own events in plain words: what was changed, and what was added to it, such as an assessment, a decision, a cost line, or a capability it serves. Changes to a sensitive field, and to cost lines, are withheld from people who may not see them. Reports → History shows every change in one place, for managers, auditors, and administrators: narrowed to a person, a record, a kind of record, or a

title: Running the program
heading: Appearance
text: Admin → Appearance makes the product yours, with a live preview: the product's name and your organization's name; a logo for light and for dark mode, and a tab icon; the default palette (Wren, Slate, or Garnet) and an accent color, which is adjusted for dark mode and refused if text on it could not be read; how scores are colored: an ordinal ramp in one hue from pale to deep, which keeps scores apart from the colors of flags, or a signal ramp from red through amber to green. Each person chooses light, dark, or system mode and a palette for themselves, from the appearance button at the top right.

title: Running the program
heading: Back up and recover
text: Back up the data home, and the database as well if you use PostgreSQL. uv run appwren program export keeps a copy of the program you have shaped. If nobody can sign in, appwren users adds an administrator or resets a password from the server's own command line. Changes made there are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Configuration
heading: Configuration
text: Configuration This guide is for whoever runs the server. It covers appwren.toml , environment overrides, the data home, single sign-on, PostgreSQL, upgrading, running behind a reverse proxy, and the guard on demo installations.

title: Configuration
heading: What is configured where
text: AppWren keeps two kinds of settings apart. Kind Where it lives Examples How the server runs appwren.toml and the environment Address, port, database, data home The program and the product's look The database, set in the app or by a program pack Vocabularies, fields, what each stage requires, the questions, the scoring model, name, logo, colors This guide is about the first. For the second, see Running the program .

title: Configuration
heading: Where the file is found
text: uv run appwren init writes a commented appwren.toml in the current directory. Every command looks for the file in this order: The --config FILE option (short form -c ), given before the command. The APPWREN_CONFIG environment variable. ./appwren.toml . uv run appwren --config /etc/appwren/appwren.toml doctor Relative paths in the file are resolved against the file's own directory, not the directory you run from. An installation therefore moves as a unit.

title: Configuration
heading: Every section and key
text: The file has four sections. Only the first three matter for a new installation; [sso] is optional. A section or key that AppWren does not know is an error, not something it ignores. Every problem in the file is reported together.

title: Configuration
heading: [server]
text: Key Default Meaning host "127.0.0.1" The address the web server listens on. Keep 127.0.0.1 when a reverse proxy on the same machine terminates TLS. Use 0.0.0.0 only behind one port 8000 The port workers 1 How many server processes to run. One is enough for SQLite and small teams base_url "" The public address people use to reach AppWren, such as "https://appwren.example.org" . Used for the single sign-on redirect address. Set it when you use single sign-on session_idle_hours 12 A sign-in ends after this long without activity session_max_days 7 A sign-in ends after this long in any case host , port , and workers can also be given to uv run appwren serve as --host , --port , and --workers , wh

title: Configuration
heading: [database]
text: Key Default Meaning url "" Empty means SQLite, in a file inside the data home. For PostgreSQL, an address beginning postgresql+psycopg:// . See Use PostgreSQL

title: Configuration
heading: [data]
text: Key Default Meaning home "var" The data home: the one directory that holds everything not in the database

title: Configuration
heading: [sso]
text: Single sign-on is optional and off until both issuer and client_id are set. See Single sign-on . Key Default Meaning issuer "" The identity provider's issuer address. For Microsoft Entra ID, "https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0" client_id "" The client (application) ID the provider gave AppWren client_secret_env "APPWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET" The name of the environment variable that holds the client secret. The secret itself is refused in the file scopes "openid profile email" What AppWren asks the provider for. Must include openid roles_claim "roles" The claim in the ID token that lists a person's application roles or groups label "Sign in with your organization account" The wo

title: Configuration
heading: Environment overrides
text: Any value can be overridden by an environment variable named APPWREN_<SECTION>_<KEY> , in capitals. The environment wins over the file. Variable Overrides APPWREN_SERVER_HOST [server] host APPWREN_SERVER_PORT [server] port APPWREN_SERVER_WORKERS [server] workers APPWREN_SERVER_BASE_URL [server] base_url APPWREN_SERVER_SESSION_IDLE_HOURS [server] session_idle_hours APPWREN_SERVER_SESSION_MAX_DAYS [server] session_max_days APPWREN_DATABASE_URL [database] url APPWREN_DATA_HOME [data] home APPWREN_SERVER_PORT=8080 uv run appwren serve APPWREN_CONFIG is separate: it names the file itself.

title: Configuration
heading: Secrets are refused in the file
text: appwren.toml is meant to be safe to read, copy, and keep under version control. AppWren refuses to start if the file holds a secret: a key that looks like a password, secret, token, or key, or a database address with a password in it. Put secrets in the environment instead. For the database, set the password in PGPASSWORD , or put the whole address, password and all, in APPWREN_DATABASE_URL .

title: Configuration
heading: The data home
text: The data home is created by init . With the default settings it is ./var . Path Holds The SQLite database When no database address is set brand/ Uploaded logos and the tab icon logs/ The server's log, rotated files/ Reserved for attachments, each stored once under the SHA-256 of its content. Nothing here is served directly exports/ Reserved for exports .appwren-home A marker that says this directory is a data home Back it up as a whole. With PostgreSQL, back up the database as well. Do not edit its contents by hand. It must be writable by the account that runs the server. Request bodies and tokens are never written to the log.

title: Configuration
heading: Single sign-on
text: You do not need this to use AppWren. A new installation signs in with an email address and a password that AppWren keeps, and an evaluation or a small team needs nothing else. Single sign-on is something an administrator adds when the organization wants people to use the account they already have, under its own multi-factor authentication and offboarding. When it is on, it sits beside local accounts and does not replace them. The sign-in page shows the organization's button first, with the password form folded beneath it. An administrator can always sign in with a password, so a provider that is down or misconfigured never locks everyone out. AppWren speaks OpenID Connect: the authorization-

title: Configuration
heading: What you set, and where
text: What Where The provider's issuer and AppWren's client ID [sso] in appwren.toml The client secret An environment variable, APPWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET unless you name another AppWren's public address [server] base_url , so the redirect address is always the same Which of the provider's roles or groups give which role here In the app: Admin → Single sign-on The redirect address to give the provider is <base_url>/api/v1/sso/callback . Admin → Single sign-on shows it, before and after you set anything up.

title: Configuration
heading: With Microsoft Entra ID
text: In the Entra admin center, open App registrations → New registration . Name it, choose Accounts in this organizational directory only , and add a Web redirect URI: your base_url followed by /api/v1/sso/callback . From the registration's Overview , copy the Application (client) ID and the Directory (tenant) ID . Under Certificates & secrets , add a client secret and copy its Value . It is shown once. Under App roles , create a role for each kind of access you want to give from Entra ID, for users and groups. The role's Value is what AppWren sees: for example AppWren.Admin , AppWren.Architect , AppWren.IT.Leader . Under Enterprise applications , open the same application, then Users and groups

title: Configuration
heading: With another provider
text: Register AppWren as a confidential web client with the redirect address above. Set issuer to the address whose /.well-known/openid-configuration the provider serves, and client_id to what it gave you. Have it put a person's groups or roles in a claim, and name that claim in roles_claim (many providers call it groups ). If the provider says email_verified is true for its addresses, leave trust_email as it is.

title: Configuration
heading: Roles from the provider
text: Admin → Single sign-on lists mappings. Each says: everyone the provider gives this value gets this role here. Role here For Works in a unit One unit. Membership grants nothing by itself; it says where a person works Steward, Leader One unit, and everything beneath it Architect, Manager The whole organization, or one unit Auditor, Administrator The whole organization Roles given this way are set again at every sign-in . Take the role away at the provider and it is gone here the next time the person signs in. A shorter session_max_days shortens the wait. Roles given by hand under Admin → People are left alone, and are shown apart from those the provider gave. The last administrator is never re

title: Configuration
heading: Who a person is
text: A person is known by the provider's own identifier for them, never by an address alone. The first time someone signs in: if an account here has the address the provider vouches for, the two are joined, and from then on the provider's identifier is what counts; otherwise an account is made for them, with the roles their mappings give, unless create_accounts is false . A disabled account cannot come in through the provider. Signing out of AppWren does not sign anyone out of the provider.

title: Configuration
heading: Passwords, once it is on
text: With local_sign_in = true , anyone who has a password may still use it. With false , only administrators may. There is no setting that removes the administrator's password, on purpose: it is the way in when the provider cannot be reached.

title: Configuration
heading: Try it on a laptop
text: scripts/dev_identity_provider.py is a stand-in provider for trying this out. It has a fixed list of people and no passwords, and its signing key is published in the file, so it proves nothing and listens only on the machine it runs on. uv run python scripts/dev_identity_provider.py Then set issuer = "http://127.0.0.1:8099" , client_id = "appwren-dev" , and trust_email = true under [sso] , and start AppWren with APPWREN_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET=dev-secret in its environment.

title: Configuration
heading: Use PostgreSQL
text: SQLite is the default and needs no setup. Use PostgreSQL when many people will use AppWren at once or you want more than one server process. The features and the data model are the same on both, and the test suite runs on both. Install the driver, which is optional: `` bash uv sync --extra postgres `` Create an empty database and a role that owns it, with your usual PostgreSQL tools. Set the address in appwren.toml , without the password: `` toml [database] url = "postgresql+psycopg://appwren@db.example.org:5432/appwren" `` Put the password in the environment, then set up and check: `` bash export PGPASSWORD=… uv run appwren init uv run appwren doctor `` Moving an existing installation from

title: Configuration
heading: Upgrade
text: After updating the code: uv sync uv run appwren db upgrade db upgrade applies any migrations the database has not had and adds anything new in the default program without overwriting what you have shaped. Coming from 0.1.0, that is the tables for interfaces, hosting, cost, and contracts, their vocabularies, and a new version of the default scoring model for installations still running the previous default; see What an upgrade does to the program . Back up first: an upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring. serve refuses to start on a schema that is behind, and uv run appwren db current shows where the database is.

title: Configuration
heading: Run behind a reverse proxy
text: AppWren speaks plain HTTP and expects a reverse proxy to terminate TLS in front of it. Keep host = "127.0.0.1" when the proxy is on the same machine. Have the proxy send X-Forwarded-Proto: https . AppWren marks its session cookie Secure when the request arrived over HTTPS, by that header or directly. Forward the Host header unchanged. Requests that change anything are refused when their origin does not match the host, which is part of the protection against requests from other sites. Requests larger than 32 MB are refused. The app sets its own security headers, including a content security policy with no inline script or style and no third-party origins, so the proxy does not need to add the

title: Configuration
heading: The demo and the network
text: A demo organization signs in anyone who asks as any of its sample people, with no password. So a demo's server listens only on the machine it runs on: serve refuses any other host, and the sample sign-in refuses requests from other machines. If you do want to show a demo to others on a network you trust: uv run appwren --config demo/appwren.toml serve --host 0.0.0.0 --demo-on-network Anyone who can reach it can then sign in as the demo's portfolio manager or administrator. Never do this with a database that holds anything real; a demo database holds nothing that is.

title: The API
heading: The API
text: API Everything the web app does, it does through a JSON API under /api/v1 . This guide covers how to sign in, how answers and errors are shaped, how lists page, and what routes there are. The exact shape of every request and answer is in the OpenAPI document: openapi.json in this directory, or /api/openapi.json on a running server. This release has no API tokens. A program signs in as an account, with that account's password, and holds a session as a browser does. Tokens scoped to a role arrive with integrations in a later release; see the roadmap . Until 1.0, routes may change between releases. Changes are listed in the changelog .

title: The API
heading: Sign in
text: curl -s -c cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"email": "you@example.org", "password": "…"}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/session The answer describes who you are, and sets a session cookie, appwren_session : { "data": { "account": {"id": 12, "name": "Your Name", "email": "you@example.org"}, "roles": ["manager", "member"], "permissions": {"…": true}, "units": {"manager": null}, "member_units": [4], "has_password": true, "csrf_token": "…" }, "meta": {} } Everyone holds member . In units , each scoped role lists the units it covers, or null for the whole organization. permissions says what the account may do somewhere, such as manage or architect ; whether it may do it to

title: The API
heading: Changing things
text: Every request that changes anything ( POST , PUT , PATCH , DELETE ) must carry the session's CSRF token in a header: curl -s -b cookies.txt -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -H 'X-CSRF-Token: …' \ -d '{"name": "Freezer Watch", "sourcing": "built_here", "lifecycle": "active", "tier": "2", "org_unit_id": 4}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/applications Without it the answer is 403. If the request carries an Origin header, it must match the host, or the request is refused.

title: The API
heading: Editing a record someone else is editing
text: Records carry a version . Send the version you read with a PATCH , and if someone else has changed the record since, the answer is 409 and nothing is saved. Read it again and decide what to do.

title: The API
heading: Answers
text: Every successful answer has the same envelope: {"data": …, "meta": {…}} data is one object or a list. meta carries what is about the answer and not in it: paging for a list, or a count of what else changed. Times are UTC in ISO 8601. Dates with no time, such as a review date, are YYYY-MM-DD .

title: The API
heading: What the API will not do
text: It never returns a record you may not see, and never counts one. It never returns a sensitive field, a cost line, or a contract you may not see, and refuses to filter or sort by a sensitive field, or to take a value for one. It never gives a total of cost that includes a part you may not see. It never fetches anything: support dates arrive only in a file someone sends. It never edits an assessment or a decision. Each is superseded by a new one. It never lets a person record a decision about an application they are accountable for. It never takes a score. Scores are worked out from the record and the answers. It never changes the history. There is no route that does.

title: Command reference
heading: Command reference
text: Command reference Every appwren command. This page is written from the program itself, so it always matches the version it ships with. Run commands with uv run appwren … from the project directory. Options that come before the command apply to all of them: appwren [-h] [--version] [-c FILE] [-v | -q] COMMAND ...

title: Command reference
heading: Commands
text: Command What it does appwren init Set up a new installation appwren serve Run the web server appwren db Look after the database schema appwren users Manage accounts from the command line appwren verify Check that the history has not been altered appwren demo Build a fictional organization to explore appwren program Move the program between installations appwren technologies Bring technology support dates in from a file appwren doctor Check that this installation is healthy

title: Command reference
heading: appwren init
text: Write a configuration file if there is none, create the data home, create or upgrade the database, and create the first administrator if there is none. Safe to run again. Option Meaning --force overwrite an existing configuration file --admin-email EMAIL create the first administrator with this address --admin-name NAME the first administrator's name --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking

title: Command reference
heading: appwren serve
text: Run AppWren's web server. It refuses to start on a database whose schema is behind; run appwren db upgrade first. Option Meaning --host address to listen on (default: from the configuration) --port PORT port to listen on (default: from the configuration) --workers WORKERS server processes (default: from the configuration) --reload restart when the code changes (development) --demo-on-network let a demo organization listen beyond this machine (anyone who reaches it can sign in as its sample people)

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db
text: Look after the database schema.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db upgrade
text: Apply any migrations the database has not had. Export first: an upgrade cannot be undone except by restoring.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren db current
text: Show which migration the database is at, and which this version expects. Exits with 1 when they differ.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users
text: Manage accounts from the command line: for setting up, and for getting back in when nobody can sign in. Everyday account management is in the app, under Admin. Changes made here are recorded in the history as made at the command line.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users add
text: Add an account. It asks for a password unless --password-stdin or --invite is given. Option Meaning EMAIL the email address the person signs in with --name the person's name --title their job title --role ROLE a role: admin, manager, architect, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE; manager and architect may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated) --unit CODE a unit they work in, by code (may be repeated) --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking --invite add them without a password: they can be named on records now, and sign in once they are given a password or use single sign-on

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users list
text: List every account with its status and roles.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users disable
text: Stop an account signing in and end its sessions. Its records and history are kept. The last active administrator cannot be disabled. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users enable
text: Let a disabled account sign in again. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users reset-password
text: Give an account a new password and end its sessions. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --password-stdin read the password from standard input instead of asking

title: Command reference
heading: appwren users roles
text: Show an account's roles, or with --set replace the roles granted in AppWren. Roles mapped from an identity provider are left alone. The last active administrator cannot lose that role. Option Meaning EMAIL the account's email address --set ROLE a role: admin, manager, architect, auditor, steward=unit:CODE, or leader=unit:CODE; manager and architect may also take unit:CODE (may be repeated); with none, removes every role

title: Command reference
heading: appwren verify
text: Recompute the hash chain over every event in the history and report the first one that does not hold. Exits with 1 if the history is broken.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren demo
text: Build the Bramblewood Institute for Health Research, a fictional organization with two years of history, in its own directory. Everything in it is made by the same code the app uses. Start it with the command it prints. Option Meaning PATH where to build it (default: ./demo) --seed SEED a different number gives a different Bramblewood --port PORT the port its server will use (default: 8020) --force rebuild a demo that is already there

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program
text: The program is everything a portfolio team configures: vocabularies, the organization's own fields, what each lifecycle stage requires, sensitive fields, the capability map, the questions, and the scoring model. It lives in the database and moves as one file.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program export
text: Write the whole program as one JSON document, to a file or to standard output. Option Meaning --output , -o FILE write to this file

title: Command reference
heading: appwren program import
text: Load a program pack. The whole pack is checked first, and nothing is loaded unless all of it can be. A vocabulary value in use is retired rather than removed, and capabilities are only ever added. Option Meaning FILE the pack to load --dry-run say what would change, and change nothing

title: Command reference
heading: appwren technologies
text: Technologies and their releases are kept in the app. Their support dates can also be brought in from a file, so that nobody types them. AppWren does not fetch the file: you bring it.

title: Command reference
heading: appwren technologies import-eol
text: Read a JSON file of end-of-life data: one object whose keys are products and whose values are lists of releases, each with a cycle and any of releaseDate, eol, extendedSupport, and latest. A product is matched to the technology whose end-of-life key it is. Releases are added and dates updated; nothing is removed. Option Meaning FILE the file to read --dry-run say what would change, and change nothing

title: Command reference
heading: appwren doctor
text: Check the configuration, the data home, the database and its schema, and the history. Exits with 1 if anything must be fixed.

title: Changelog
heading: Changelog
text: Changelog AppWren follows semantic versioning. Each wave of the roadmap is a release. Before 1.0, a release may contain breaking changes; they are listed under Breaking .

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: The documentation site. The guides, with their pictures of the demo organization, are published at https://robert-mcdermott.github.io/appwren/ : a home page, one page for each guide, the changelog, an API reference written from the OpenAPI document, search, and light and dark themes. node scripts/site/build.mjs builds it from docs/ with Node 22 and no packages, and fails on a broken link, anchor, or picture; node scripts/site/audit.mjs checks every page in both themes at desk and phone widths.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 2, The landscape : each application in its surroundings. What it sends and receives and what data passes, what depends on it and what breaks if it goes, where it runs, what it costs and what pays, the contracts behind it, what else does the same job, and what it is built on that is falling out of support. Upgrade with uv sync and uv run appwren db upgrade . Every row and file is kept.

text: Interfaces. Data passing from one application to another is a record of its own, with a reference ( INT-0007 ), a method, how often, the classes of data it carries, and an owner. An application's new Connections part shows what it sends and receives. An interface is seen by whoever may see both of its applications and kept by whoever keeps either. Data flows. Landscape → Data flows follows a class of data between applications, and marks any interface that delivers a class the receiving application's record does not list. How a record is connected. Every application, component, capability, technology, vendor, and interface opens a picture of what it is joined to, with any neighbor opened a ri

title: Changelog
heading: Changed
text: An application that receives data through an interface now counts among the dependents of the application that sends it, so recording interfaces can raise a source's business value. The default scoring model has a new version. Cost and burden is now annual cost 30, cost per user 15, license use 10, support effort 25, and change effort 20, so scores for cost and burden move. An installation still running the previous default gets the new one on upgrade; one that has shaped its model keeps it, and can take the new factors from the default program when it chooses. A record's history names the vendor, application, or person a change refers to, where it showed a number.

title: Changelog
heading: Fixed
text: A record's history told an assessment, a decision, a capability served, and a unit that uses an application each as "Added this application". Each is now told for what it is, and the copy of a decision onto its application is no longer told as a second change.

title: Changelog
text: Wave 1, The portfolio : install, sign in, and keep one record of every application, with what it is built on and what it does for the organization; assess it, read four scores with their working, see the recommendation and its rule, and record what people decided.

title: Changelog
heading: Added
text: Foundation. appwren init , serve , db upgrade , db current , verify , and doctor . Deployment settings in appwren.toml with environment overrides; secrets are refused in the file. SQLite by default and PostgreSQL by address, on one model and one set of migrations. Every change is written to an append-only, hash-chained history in the same transaction, and appwren verify finds the first event that has been altered. Accounts and roles. Local accounts with scrypt-hashed passwords, server-side sessions, CSRF protection, and throttled sign-in. Seven roles: admin, manager, architect, auditor, leader, steward, and member, some limited to a unit and everything beneath it. Every API route is checked
